extracted.intended_audience: scholars and practitioners interested in peer review, research funding panels, and science & technology studies (e.g., academic reviewers, program officers, STS researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and understanding how grant/fellowship review panels judge proposals: the criteria they invoke, the disciplinary/epistemological differences that shape judgments, the informal signals that affect outcomes, and the deliberative rules panels use to reach consensus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria of excellence (clarity, originality, significance, quality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Panels were required to rank submissions according to criteria of excellence as spelled out by funding organizations, typically using terms like clarity, originality, significance, or quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These terms are often unclear and contested among panelists and officials; they do not by themselves allow transparent ranking. Interpreting these criteria requires group discussion and continuous reasoning about what each term means in the specific context of the proposal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive contextualization
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule that applications should be evaluated according to the criteria of the discipline from which they originate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panelists bring disciplinary pictures of excellence but—under many conditions—are willing to respect the sovereignty of other disciplines and defer to disciplinary expertise. Cognitive contextualization is a primary customary rule guiding deliberations and helps panels justify discipline-specific standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive epistemological style
rubrics_metrics.description: An epistemological style that 'values verstehen, attention to details, and contextual specificity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common in humanities, history, and social sciences clusters; leads evaluators to privilege deep contextual understanding and nuanced, detail-rich work when judging proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructivist epistemological style
rubrics_metrics.description: An epistemological style that 'emphasizes proposals that ‘give voice’ to various groups.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators with this style favor research that foregrounds perspectives of marginalized or particular groups and values interpretive, voice-centered contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positivist epistemological style
rubrics_metrics.description: An epistemological style that 'favors generalizability and hypothesis testing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More prevalent in social sciences; leads reviewers to value methodological rigor aimed at producing generalizable findings and hypothesis-driven research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utilitarian epistemological style
rubrics_metrics.description: An epistemological style that 'values only the production of instrumental knowledge.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators with this orientation prioritize practical or instrumental outcomes and the usefulness of research for policy, practice, or tangible applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basis of originality judgment: approach vs method
rubrics_metrics.description: Different disciplines use different bases when judging originality: humanities and history often judge originality by a project's approach, whereas social scientists more often judge originality by method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When preparing proposals or assessing originality, match claims about originality to the evaluative concerns of the discipline (e.g., emphasize conceptual approach in humanities; emphasize methodological novelty in many social sciences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal/evanescent criteria (signs of intelligence, elegance, cultural capital, moral qualities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria not explicitly required by funders but that play an important role in reviewers' impressions: signs of intelligence, elegance, cultural capital, and the applicant's moral qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These soft signals can influence evaluations alongside formal criteria. They are informal, often unspoken, and can affect perceptions of the person behind the proposal as much as the proposal itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdisciplinarity and diversity as evaluative priorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Some funding organizations and reviewers favor interdisciplinarity and diversity, even where this may counter a narrow notion of excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels or organizations may explicitly or implicitly reward proposals that demonstrate cross-disciplinary reach or contribute to diversity goals; proposers should signal such dimensions when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatic fairness / customary rules of deliberation
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of implicit deliberative rules (termed 'pragmatic fairness') that panels follow to reach consensus during discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These customary rules include respecting discipline-specific criteria, deferring to expertise, negotiating meanings of criteria, and using deliberation itself as a source of trust. They are rarely explicitly stated but structure how panels move from disagreement to a ranking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel composition and program officer roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal and informal considerations about how panel members are selected and what is expected of them, and the tasks of program officers in shaping panels and the review process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection procedures, expectations about panelists' duties, and program officer practices materially shape how criteria are applied; awareness of these procedural elements is important for both panel design and applicants' strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal preferences and idiosyncrasies of reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers' personal preferences and idiosyncrasies play an important and unavoidable role in evaluations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The deliberation process and customary rules reduce but cannot eliminate individual subjectivity; panels cannot fully subsume qualitatively incommensurate proposals under a single standard, so variability across reviewers persists and can shape outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for group discussion to negotiate meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: Because evaluative terms (clarity, originality, significance, quality) have multiple meanings, panels rely on interactive group discussion to create shared interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions about excellence emerge from negotiation during deliberation; transparent application of criteria requires collective reasoning about what each criterion will mean for the specific set of proposals.
